one_paragraph_summary: Delivered September 16, 2006 as the inaugural lecture at the Dr. Jovito R. Salonga Center for Law and Development, Silliman University College of Law, this address by CJP opens by congratulating Silliman for institutionalizing Salonga's 'deep-seated compassion for the poor and the downtrodden' through 'transformative law -- which means harnessing the law to transform society and to improve the lives of the people.' He presents the UNDP definition of access to justice: 'the ability of people to seek and obtain a remedy through formal or informal institutions of justice, and in conformity with human rights standards.' A 2004 UNDP survey of Philippine private legal practitioners found: lawyering for the poor had 'urban bias'; courts located mostly in urban centers; for the rural poor, physical inaccessibility posed difficulties; 'loss of income appeared to be the strongest deterrent to lawyering for the poor, especially among young and new lawyers.' The UNDP connects access to poverty eradication: 'groups such as the poor and disadvantaged who suffer from discrimination also often fall victim to criminal and illegal acts... it is harder for them to seek redress.' He presents the SC's access initiatives: exempted poor litigants from docket fees; Justice on Wheels (December 21, 2004; mobile courts bring justice to inaccessible places); pro-poor, pro-labor, pro-human rights decisions; Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Comelec ('party-list system is reserved for the poor and the marginalized'). He frames the liberty-and-prosperity philosophy as 'directed primarily to assist the poor, the marginalized and the disadvantaged' and closes: 'I urge you to contribute fully and meaningfully to discussions, bearing in mind that the results of this conference will lay the groundwork for the forthcoming Global Conference on Liberty and Prosperity scheduled on October 18-20, 2006. During that global gathering, we hope to spread the gospel of Liberty and Prosperity beyond our shores and unto the world.'
